claim: When the formatted type T carries its own contract attributes, they are ignored. With no SurrogateType, Collect always calls CreateContractlessMembers(type), which serializes every public read-write member by name. As a result, [MessagePackObject]/[Key]/[IgnoreMember] and [DataContract]/[DataMember] on T are never read. A member marked [IgnoreMember], or a member left out of a [DataContract], is still serialized. This breaks the acceptance criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured' and the maintainer's 'if there is no [DataContract] or [MessagePackObject] attribute ... go contractless', which implies contractless only when those attributes are absent.

claim: The requirement says MessagePack attributes on T are honoured when present. GeneratedFormatterCollector.Collect never reads them: with no surrogate it always calls CreateContractlessMembers, which takes every public read-write member sorted by name and uses string keys. As a result, [MessagePackObject]/[Key(n)] int keys, keyAsPropertyName settings and [IgnoreMember] on T are all ignored. Example: Lib.Data has [MessagePackObject], [Key(0)] Value and [IgnoreMember] SecretToken. The generated formatter writes a string-keyed map that includes SecretToken. This leaks a member the type marked as ignored and produces a wire format that does not match the type's declared contract.

claim: Collect never checks whether another formatter already exists for the same data type. Two [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] classes targeting the same T both produce an ObjectSerializationInfo for T. So does a generated formatter for a T that also carries [MessagePackObject] in the same compilation, which TypeCollector also emits. Both models are merged into the resolver. Depending on how ObjectInfos are merged, either the resolver registers T twice (a duplicate key in the resolver lookup at run time), or one model is silently dropped. If it is dropped, the user's partial class gets no body and fails with CS0535. No diagnostic is reported.

claim: Only the formatter class itself is checked for 'partial' (IsPartial) and nothing checks the formatter's own accessibility. A formatter nested in a non-partial outer class makes the generated nesting declaration conflict with the user's outer class (CS0260/CS0101). A private or protected nested formatter is referenced from the generated resolver, which cannot access it (CS0122). In both cases the user gets a generated-code compile error instead of MsgPack019 or a dedicated diagnostic.

claim: In contractless mode only public read-write members are collected, and constructorParameters is always empty. A struct whose public state is get-only and set through a constructor (for example readonly struct Point { int X {get;} int Y {get;} }) gets a formatter with zero members. It serializes as an empty map and deserializes as default(T), silently losing all data, with no diagnostic. The existing DynamicContractlessObjectResolver serializes such members and uses the constructor. Classes with get-only properties likewise drop them silently, and positional records are rejected with MsgPack007.

claim: The GeneratorUtilities.cs filter excludes attributed formatters from the hand-written formatter list only when the attribute matches by display string. For existing users, nothing changes. However, the template now emits 'partial class' with no accessibility for user-declared formatters, and the collected ObjectSerializationInfo is registered in the generated resolver. The resolver will instantiate the formatter via 'new Formatter()'. If the user's partial class is public, has a constructor, or is nested, the generated resolver references it without checks. If the class is declared private or nested private, the generated resolver cannot access it, producing compile errors in the user's project.

claim: Contractless members are ordered by ordinal name and read-only or get-only members are silently dropped. The wire format therefore depends on member names. Adding a member to T in Project A changes the int-key positions and the string keys, which is fine for string keys. The model also sets isIntKey=false, so string-key maps are used. However, in surrogate mode with all-int keys, IntKey comes from the surrogate while members that lack a Key are silently skipped, rather than being treated as errors the way MsgPack004 treats [MessagePackObject] types. This is a design choice rather than a break for existing users.
